title: The house of the Aziz
hook: the lady of the house tries to seduce him, and he says: I seek refuge in Allah

segments.voice: Yesterday: sold for a few coins, and a boy the traders thought little of. Your line was the price they paid isn't your worth. Did you catch a low price on anyone? Day sixty.
screen: `THE PRICE THEY PAID ISN'T YOUR WORTH.`

segments.voice: Temptation rarely arrives when you're weak and alone in a dark alley. More often it shows up when life is finally going well. You've got the job, the trust, the key to the building. Nobody's watching. Yusuf has grown up in the house of the man who bought him. The Qur'an calls that man al-Aziz, a title, something like the mighty one, a high official of Egypt. Yusuf has reached his full strength, and the verse says he's been given wisdom and knowledge. He's trusted, he's handsome, he lives under their roof. And the lady of the house has noticed. Today: the house of the Aziz.
screen: `TEMPTATION WHEN THINGS GO WELL.` → `AL-AZIZ, A HIGH OFFICIAL.` → `THE LADY OF THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf, verse twenty-three, told with great restraint. She, in whose house he was, tried to turn him from himself. She closed the doors, and said: come. And Yusuf's answer, in Pickthall's old translation: "I seek refuge in Allah!" In Arabic, ma'adha-llah. Then he gives his reasons: he's my master, he's treated me well; and wrongdoers don't prosper. Who does he mean by my master? Commentators split. Some say the Aziz, the man who gave him a good home. Others say his Lord, Allah. The Arabic word, rabb, can carry both, and the verse may be holding both at once: loyalty to the man who trusted him, and to the God who made him. Then comes a verse commentators read in more than one way: she desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the clear sign of his Lord. What was the sign? The Qur'an doesn't say. Commentators have offered many answers; the text stays silent. What it does say is that Yusuf was human, the pull was real, and he turned. That phrase, I seek refuge in Allah, has a close cousin in daily Muslim life: a'udhu billah. The Qur'an tells its readers to seek refuge in Allah before reciting, and Muslims also say it when anger rises, or a bad thought knocks. Seeking refuge is not proving you're strong. It's admitting you need a place to run to, and running there. Yusuf didn't argue with the temptation, or try to out-think it. He named where he was going, and he went.
screen: `SHE CLOSED THE DOORS.` · `I SEEK REFUGE IN ALLAH!` · `MY MASTER — THE MAN, OR GOD?` · `THE SIGN OF HIS LORD.` · then, large: `A'UDHU BILLAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your refuge before the knock. Settle, and breathe. Think of the thing that tempts you most often. It might be small: the extra drink, the cruel comment, the scroll at two in the morning, the lie that would make things easier. Picture it knocking. Now, instead of arguing with it, picture turning and walking to somewhere safe. If you pray, you can say a'udhu billah, I seek refuge in Allah, and let the words be the door you step through. If not, choose one word that means safe to you, and practice going there. The bell holds the time.
The house of the Aziz. Where Yusuf, trusted and tempted behind closed doors, said: I seek refuge in Allah. Today's word.
screen: `THE HOUSE OF THE AZIZ — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I seek refuge. When temptation knocks today, don't argue with it; just turn and go to your refuge. Day sixty.

howItsDone: Muslims say a'udhu billah, "I seek refuge in Allah," before reciting the Qur'an, when angry, and when tempted; Yusuf's words in the house of the Aziz are a well-known example.

fork.setup: you're Yusuf. the doors are closed, nobody is watching, and the lady of the house says: come. what do you say?
fork.reveal: ma'adha-llah: I seek refuge in Allah. then his reasons: my master has treated me well, and wrongdoers don't prosper.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 12:23: "I seek refuge in Allah" — a close cousin of a'udhu billah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a scandal.
what it means: a trusted young man, really tempted, who doesn't argue with it but runs to refuge in Allah.
what a scholar hears: "he is my rabb" in 12:23 is read by some as the Aziz, his master, and by others as Allah; 12:24's burhan, the sign, is left unexplained.

sources.ref: Qur'an 16:98 (seek refuge in Allah before reciting)

notes: Only 'I seek refuge in Allah!' is quoted from Pickthall 1930 (12:23); please verify wording and punctuation.

12:24 ('she desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord'): translations and commentators differ significantly on this verse, including whether Yusuf 'desired' at all. The script gives one common reading and says the sign is unexplained. A Keeper should review this carefully.
Al-Aziz glossed as 'a title, something like the great one, a high official'. The wife is unnamed in the Qur'an (later tradition: Zulaykha); the script doesn't name her.
Two readings of 'my rabb' (the Aziz / Allah) given without ranking. Confirm.
Tone kept suitable for all ages; confirm.
